title: Ethereum & Smart Contracts
tagline: Understand the world computer, read real Solidity, deploy to a test network and think like an auditor
summary: From accounts and gas to your first Solidity contract: the Ethereum model, the EVM and the fee market, reading and writing small contracts, calls versus transactions, patterns and the reentrancy trap, and testing and deploying safely. Code examples were compiled and checked; you run them yourself in the free Remix editor.

modules.title: The Ethereum model
modules.summary: Accounts, transactions, blocks and units: the building blocks of the world computer.
modules.outcome: You can describe the two account types, read the fields of a transaction, convert between wei, gwei and ether and explain how Ethereum differs from Bitcoin.
modules.intro: Ethereum is often called a 'world computer': a single shared machine whose state is agreed by thousands of nodes. To write programs for it you need a precise model of what that machine contains and how it changes.

topics.title: Accounts and state
topics.html:
Ethereum keeps a world state: a mapping from addresses to accounts. Every account has a balance, a nonce (a count of how many transactions it has sent), and, for contracts, code and storage. A transaction is the only thing that changes this state.

Two kinds of account
Externally owned account (EOA)Contract account
Controlled byA private keyIts code
Has codeNoYes
Can start a transactionYesNo; only reacts when called
Created byGenerating a key pairA deployment transaction
Typical useA person's walletAn application's rules and assets

Check what you just learned

1. Which kind of account can start a transaction?
  • Contract accounts
  • Both
  • Externally owned accounts (correct)
  • Neither

Contracts only react to calls.

Tip

The nonce stops a transaction from being replayed: each EOA transaction must carry the next number in sequence.

Check what you just learned

1. A contract account is controlled by:
  • A private key
  • A bank
  • A miner
  • Its code (correct)

The code decides what happens.
keyPoints: Ethereum's world state maps addresses to accounts.
Only EOAs start transactions; contracts react.

topics.title: Transactions
topics.html:
Fields of a transaction
FieldMeaning
nonceThe sender's transaction count, to order and prevent replay
toThe recipient: an EOA or a contract (empty when deploying)
valueHow much ETH to send, in wei
dataEncoded function call and arguments for a contract, or contract code when deploying
gasLimitThe most gas the sender allows this transaction to use
maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGasThe most the sender will pay per gas, and the tip for the block producer
signatureProves the sender authorised it
chainIdWhich network it is for, to stop replay on other chains
Worked example

Three kinds of transaction

What do the fields look like?

  1. Plain transfer: to = a friend's address, value = 0.1 ETH, data empty.
  2. Contract call: to = the contract, value = 0 (or some ETH), data = the encoded function call.
  3. Deployment: to empty, data = the compiled contract code.

Answer. Everything on Ethereum is a transaction with a different shape.

Wei, gwei and ether

Contracts count in wei because they cannot hold decimals. Change the amount of ETH to see it in gwei and wei.

Adjust Amount in ETH and see Gwei, Wei (shown in millions) change.

Check what you just learned

1. Which field tells a contract which function to run and with what arguments?
  • data (correct)
  • value
  • nonce
  • chainId

It carries the encoded call.

Check what you just learned

1. A deployment transaction has:
  • A zero value only
  • An empty to field and code in data (correct)
  • No data
  • No signature

That creates a new contract.
keyPoints: A transaction has nonce, to, value, data, gas fields and a signature.
A contract call puts the encoded function call in data.

topics.title: Blocks, ETH and how it differs from Bitcoin
topics.html:
Ethereum compared with Bitcoin
BitcoinEthereum
Account modelUnspent outputsAccounts with balances
ProgramsLimited scriptsTuring-complete smart contracts
Block timeAbout 10 minutes12 seconds (in slots)
ConsensusProof of workProof of stake since September 2022
FeesBy transaction sizeBy computation (gas)
Native assetBTCETH, used for fees and staking

Ethereum divides time into slots of 12 seconds. In each slot a validator is chosen to propose a block, and others attest to it. After enough attestations, blocks become final. The result is much faster confirmation than Bitcoin's, with a programming model that supports applications.

Test networks

  • Test networks such as Sepolia copy Ethereum's behaviour with worthless test ETH.
  • You get test ETH from a 'faucet', a website that gives small amounts for free.
  • Always develop and practise on a test network first; mistakes there cost nothing.
  • Networks and faucets change over time, so check the official documentation for current ones.

Check what you just learned

1. Ethereum's consensus mechanism today is:
  • Proof of work
  • Voting by banks
  • Proof of stake (correct)
  • None

Since the Merge in 2022.

Check what you just learned

1. Test ETH is obtained from:
  • A bank
  • An exchange
  • Mining at home
  • A faucet (correct)

It is free and worthless.

Key terms: flip and sort

World state
All accounts and their data
EOA
Externally owned account
Contract account
An account controlled by code
Nonce
A transaction counter
Wei
The smallest unit of ether
Faucet
A site giving free test ETH
keyPoints: Ethereum has 12-second slots and proof of stake.
Test networks let you practise with worthless ETH.

modules.title: The EVM and gas
modules.summary: How contract code runs, why every operation costs gas and how the fee market works.
modules.outcome: You can explain the EVM, distinguish storage from memory and calldata and calculate a transaction fee from gas used, base fee and tip.
modules.intro: Every node must run every contract call and reach the same answer. That is only possible if computation is deterministic and metered. The Ethereum Virtual Machine and its gas system are how Ethereum achieves both.

topics.title: The Ethereum Virtual Machine
topics.html:
Definition

EVM. The Ethereum Virtual Machine: a simple, deterministic machine that executes contract bytecode. Every node runs the same instructions on the same inputs and must get the same result.

You write contracts in a high-level language such as Solidity. A compiler turns your code into bytecode, a sequence of low-level instructions called opcodes. The EVM runs those opcodes on a stack, reading and writing three kinds of data.

Where data lives
LocationLifetimeCostUse
StoragePermanent, part of the accountHighest: writing a new slot is very expensiveState variables such as balances
MemoryOnly while the call runsLowTemporary working data
CalldataOnly during the call, read-onlyCheapest to readInputs to external functions
StackOnly while the call runsVery lowSmall values used by opcodes

Check what you just learned

1. What does the compiler produce that the EVM executes?
  • Bytecode (correct)
  • A wallet
  • A hash
  • A signature

Opcodes run on the EVM.

Watch out

Because every node repeats every execution, contracts cannot use anything non-deterministic, such as the local time of one machine or true randomness from outside, without a specially designed source.

Check what you just learned

1. Which location is permanent and most expensive to write?
  • Memory
  • Storage (correct)
  • Calldata
  • Stack

Writes change the chain's state.
keyPoints: Solidity compiles to bytecode that the deterministic EVM executes.
Storage is permanent and expensive; memory and calldata are temporary and cheaper.

topics.title: Gas: metering computation
topics.html:
Each opcode has a fixed gas cost, based roughly on the work it forces nodes to do. A simple addition costs very little; writing to storage costs a great deal; sending a transaction has a base cost of 21,000 gas. Gas does two jobs: it pays block producers, and it stops infinite loops, because a transaction that runs out of gas is stopped and its changes are undone.

Rough gas costs (order of magnitude)
OperationApproximate gas
Basic transfer of ETH21,000
Addition or comparisonA few
Reading a storage valueA few hundred to a couple of thousand
Writing a new storage value (zero to non-zero)About 20,000
Updating an existing storage valueA few thousand
Emitting an eventA few thousand, depending on data
Deploying a small contractHundreds of thousands
Definition

Gas limit and gas used. The gas limit is the most gas you allow a transaction to consume. Gas used is what it actually consumed. You pay for gas used, and any unused part of the limit is refunded; if the transaction needs more than the limit it fails and you still pay for what it used.

Common mistakes

  • Setting a gas limit too low and having the transaction fail while still paying.
  • Writing to storage in a loop without thinking about cost.
  • Assuming all operations cost the same.

Check what you just learned

1. What happens if a transaction runs out of gas?
  • It is completed anyway
  • The block is deleted
  • It stops, its changes are undone and you still pay for the gas used (correct)
  • You get a refund of all gas

Work done must be paid for.

Check what you just learned

1. A basic ETH transfer costs:
  • Nothing
  • 1 gas
  • 1 million gas
  • 21,000 gas (correct)

The standard base cost.
keyPoints: Gas meters computation and prevents infinite loops.
Storage writes are the most expensive operations.

topics.title: The fee market (EIP-1559)
topics.html:
Before 2021 users bid blindly in an auction for block space. The London upgrade introduced EIP-1559: the protocol sets a base fee per gas that rises when blocks are more than half full and falls when they are emptier. The base fee is burned (destroyed), and the user can add a priority fee (a tip) to encourage the block producer to include the transaction sooner.

Formula · The fee

fee = gas used × (base fee + priority fee)

Gas used 65,000, base fee 30 gwei and tip 2 gwei: 65,000 × 32 = 2,080,000 gwei = 0.00208 ETH.

Fee calculator

Change gas used, base fee and tip to see the total fee and how much is burned. The ETH price is a teaching figure.

Adjust Gas used, Base fee (gwei), Priority fee (gwei), Price of 1 ETH (rupees) and see Total fee (ETH), Burned (ETH), Total fee (rupees) change.

Why it is better
BenefitHow
Predictable feesA visible base fee instead of guessing
Less overpayingYou pay the base fee plus a small tip
Value to all ETH holdersBurning reduces supply as usage grows

Check what you just learned

1. What happens to the base fee under EIP-1559?
  • It is burned (correct)
  • It goes to the block producer
  • It is refunded
  • It goes to a bank

Only the tip goes to the producer.

Check what you just learned

1. The priority fee is:
  • Burned
  • A tip for the block producer (correct)
  • A refund
  • Paid to a bank

It encourages inclusion.

Key terms: flip and sort

EVM
The machine that runs contract bytecode
Bytecode
Compiled low-level instructions
Opcode
A single EVM instruction
Gas
The unit of computation cost
Base fee
A protocol-set fee per gas that is burned
Priority fee
A tip to the block producer
keyPoints: Fee = gas used × (base fee + tip).
The base fee is burned; the tip pays the producer.

modules.title: Your first smart contract
modules.summary: Read and write small Solidity contracts: state, functions, events and the view and pure keywords.
modules.outcome: You can read a small contract, say what every line does and write a simple one in Remix.
modules.intro: Time to read real code. This module walks through two tiny contracts line by line. You can follow along without installing anything by using Remix, a free development environment that runs in your browser at remix.ethereum.org.

topics.title: Anatomy of a contract
topics.html:
Here is a complete contract. It stores one number, lets anyone change it and lets anyone read it. Read it first, then we will go through it.

Line by line
CodeMeaning
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MITA machine-readable licence label, required by the compiler as a warning if missing
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;Compile with version 0.8.20 or a later 0.8.x release
contract SimpleStorage { ... }Declares a contract, like a class: it has state and functions
uint256 private value;A state variable: an unsigned 256-bit integer stored permanently in the contract; private means other contracts cannot read it directly
event ValueChanged(address indexed by, uint256 newValue);Declares a log entry that apps can listen to; indexed makes 'by' searchable
function set(uint256 newValue) externalA function anyone can call from outside; it changes state
emit ValueChanged(msg.sender, newValue);Writes the log entry; msg.sender is the account that called
function get() external view returns (uint256)A read-only function that returns the stored number

Check what you just learned

1. What does the keyword view promise?
  • The function costs nothing always
  • The function is private
  • The function does not change state (correct)
  • The function is payable

It may read but not write.

Tip

Open Remix, create a file called SimpleStorage.sol, paste the code and press Compile. A green tick means it compiled.

Check what you just learned

1. msg.sender is:
  • The contract's address
  • The fee
  • The miner
  • The account that called the function (correct)

The direct caller.
keyPoints: A contract has state variables, events and functions.
view functions read state but do not change it.

topics.title: Types, functions and visibility
topics.html:
Key ideas from Counter
IdeaExampleMeaning
Public state variableuint256 public count;The compiler creates a free getter function called count()
State-changing functionincrement()Costs gas when called in a transaction
Pure functionadd(a, b)Uses only its inputs; can be called for free
Compound assignmentcount += 1Same as count = count + 1
Common types
TypeWhat it holds
uint256 and other uint sizesNon-negative whole numbers
int256Whole numbers that can be negative
booltrue or false
addressA 20-byte account address
string and bytesText and raw data
mapping(K => V)A lookup table, like a dictionary
struct and arraysGroups and lists of values
Function visibility
KeywordWho can call
externalOnly from outside the contract
publicFrom outside and inside
internalOnly this contract and contracts that inherit from it
privateOnly this contract

Since Solidity 0.8, arithmetic is checked: if an addition would overflow a uint256, the transaction reverts instead of silently wrapping around. This removed a whole category of older bugs, though you can still opt out with unchecked blocks when you are sure.

Check what you just learned

1. What does uint256 public count; create automatically?
  • A getter function named count() (correct)
  • A fee
  • An event
  • A constructor

Public state variables get free getters.

Check what you just learned

1. A pure function:
  • Reads state
  • Neither reads nor changes state (correct)
  • Changes state
  • Sends ETH

It uses only its inputs.
keyPoints: Public variables get automatic getters.
Since 0.8, arithmetic reverts on overflow.

topics.title: Events and a first run in Remix
topics.html:
Events are how contracts talk to the outside world. Storage cannot be watched cheaply, but logs can: an app can subscribe to an event and update its screen whenever one is emitted. They are also cheap compared with storage, so they are used for history that the contract itself does not need to read.

What to look for

  1. After set(42), the log shows ValueChanged with your address and 42.
  2. get() returns 42 and costs nothing because it is a call.
  3. set shows a gas figure, because it changed storage.
  4. Change the value twice and notice that the second write is cheaper than the first.
Watch out

Remix's built-in environment uses fake accounts and fake ETH. When you connect Remix to a real wallet, double-check the network. Practise on a test network first.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use events rather than storage for history?
  • They are slower
  • They are secret
  • They are much cheaper and easy for apps to follow (correct)
  • They are required

Logs cost less than storage.

Check what you just learned

1. After calling set(42), where would you see ValueChanged?
  • In the gas price
  • In your wallet balance
  • In the compiler
  • In the transaction's logs (correct)

Events appear in the receipt's logs.

Key terms: flip and sort

Solidity
The main language for Ethereum contracts
State variable
A value stored permanently in a contract
Event
A log entry apps can follow
view
Reads state but does not change it
pure
Uses neither state nor chain data
Remix
A browser-based Solidity IDE
keyPoints: Events are cheap logs that apps can follow.
Practise in Remix's built-in environment before using a test network.

modules.title: Interacting with contracts
modules.summary: Calls versus transactions, the ABI, payable functions and a first contract that holds money.
modules.outcome: You can tell reads from writes, explain the ABI and msg.value, and read a contract that accepts and pays out ETH.
modules.intro: A contract is useful when other accounts can use it. This module explains how outside accounts and apps talk to contracts, and then walks through a contract that really holds and moves ETH.

topics.title: Calls, transactions and the ABI
topics.html:
Two ways of using a function
CallTransaction
Changes stateNoYes
Needs a signatureNoYes
Costs gas to the callerNo (a node just runs it)Yes
Returns a value to youYes, immediatelyNo; you get a receipt and can read events
Exampleget() or balanceOf(address)set(5), tip(), transfer(...)
Definition

ABI. The Application Binary Interface: a description of a contract's functions and events (names, input types, output types). Wallets and libraries use it to encode a call into the data field and to decode results and logs.

A transaction's data field starts with a four-byte function selector: the first four bytes of the hash of the function's signature, for example set(uint256). Then come the arguments, encoded in a fixed format. The contract reads the selector to decide which function to run. Without the ABI, the data looks like unreadable hex.

A function selector is a hash

Ethereum uses Keccak-256 for this; the lab uses SHA-256, a different function, so the result will not match a real selector. The idea is the same: a short fingerprint of the function's signature picks the function.

Type any text and see its SHA-256 fingerprint change completely when one letter changes.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a wallet need to turn set(42) into the data bytes?
  • The contract's ABI (correct)
  • A password
  • A hash of the user
  • A faucet

The ABI describes the functions.

Check what you just learned

1. A function selector is:
  • A password
  • The first four bytes of a hash of the signature (correct)
  • A fee
  • A token

It tells the contract which function to run.
keyPoints: Calls read for free; transactions change state and cost gas.
The ABI describes functions so that calls can be encoded and decoded.

topics.title: A contract that holds ETH
topics.html:
Contracts have balances, just like wallets. A function marked payable can receive ETH sent with the call, and inside the function the amount is available as msg.value. Here is a small contract that accepts tips and lets its owner withdraw them.

What to notice
FeatureExplanation
address public immutable owner;Set once in the constructor and never changed; immutable values are cheaper than storage
mapping(address => uint256) public tipsFrom;A table of how much each address tipped; the public keyword creates a getter
function tip() external payablepayable lets it receive ETH
require(msg.value > 0, "Send some ETH");Rejects empty tips and reverts with a message
if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner();A custom error: cheaper than a text message
(bool ok, ) = owner.call{value: amount}("");Sends ETH and returns whether it worked; the result must be checked
emit Tipped / WithdrawnLogs for apps to display the history
Watch out

Never send ETH to an address and ignore whether it worked. Always check the success flag, and think about what happens if the recipient is a contract.

Check what you just learned

1. What does the payable keyword allow?
  • The function is private
  • The function is free
  • The function can receive ETH (correct)
  • The function returns a value

Without it, sending ETH reverts.

Check what you just learned

1. immutable means:
  • Public
  • Changing every block
  • Stored in memory
  • Set once at deployment and cheap to read (correct)

Fixed at construction.
keyPoints: payable functions receive ETH; msg.value is the amount.
Always check the result when sending ETH out.

topics.title: Reading a contract on an explorer
topics.html:
Block explorers show any contract's address, balance, transactions and, if the author has verified it, its source code. Reading real contracts is one of the best ways to learn.

What to check on a contract page
ItemWhat it tells you
Verified source codeWhether you can read what it does; unverified contracts deserve suspicion
Read contract tabThe free calls you can make, such as owner() and balances
Write contract tabThe transactions you could send
Transactions and eventsHow it is being used
Creator and creation transactionWho deployed it and when
Proxy informationWhether the code can be upgraded

A safe reading routine

  1. Find the owner and see whether they can move funds.
  2. Look for functions that only the owner can call and ask what they do.
  3. Check whether it is upgradable and who controls the upgrade.
  4. Search for audits and read the findings.
  5. Never interact with a contract you do not understand using your main wallet.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is verified source code important?
  • Anyone can read what the contract does (correct)
  • It makes the contract faster
  • It changes the owner
  • It lowers fees

Transparency allows scrutiny.

Check what you just learned

1. An unverified contract is:
  • Always safe
  • Harder to trust because its code is not published (correct)
  • Cheaper
  • Official

You cannot read the source.

Key terms: flip and sort

Call
A free read of contract data
Transaction
A signed, state-changing action
ABI
Description of a contract's interface
Function selector
Four bytes identifying a function
payable
A function that can receive ETH
msg.value
The ETH sent with a call
keyPoints: Explorers show verified code, read and write functions, and events.
Check ownership, upgradability and audits before interacting.

modules.title: Patterns, pitfalls and limits
modules.summary: Access control, input checks, the reentrancy trap and what smart contracts cannot do.
modules.outcome: You can apply access control and validation, recognise and fix a reentrancy bug and explain the main limits of on-chain code.
modules.intro: Smart contracts hold real value and cannot be patched casually, so a few safe habits matter more than clever tricks. This module teaches the habits that prevent most beginner losses.

topics.title: Access control and validation
topics.html:
The habits

  1. Decide who may call each function and write the check explicitly.
  2. Use msg.sender, never tx.origin, for permission checks.
  3. Validate inputs at the start with require or custom errors.
  4. Fail loudly: a revert is better than quietly doing nothing.
  5. Keep functions small and single-purpose.
  6. Emit events for every important change.
Revert styles
StyleExampleNotes
require with messagerequire(msg.value > 0, "Send some ETH");Readable, a little more gas
Custom errorif (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner();Cheaper and can carry data
assertassert(total >= part);For things that should never be false; indicates a bug
Worked example

Why tx.origin is wrong

A contract checks require(tx.origin == owner).

  1. The owner is tricked into calling a malicious contract.
  2. That contract calls the protected contract.
  3. tx.origin is still the owner, so the check passes.
  4. msg.sender would have been the malicious contract, and the check would have failed.

Answer. Use msg.sender for authorisation.

Check what you just learned

1. Which should be used to check who is calling a function?
  • tx.origin
  • block.number
  • msg.sender (correct)
  • address(this)

msg.sender is the direct caller.

Check what you just learned

1. A custom error compared with a require message is:
  • More expensive
  • The same
  • Not allowed
  • Usually cheaper (correct)

Less data is stored.
keyPoints: Check permissions with msg.sender and validate inputs early.
tx.origin authorisation can be exploited.

topics.title: The reentrancy trap
topics.html:
Reentrancy is the bug behind some of the most famous contract losses. When your contract sends ETH to another contract, that contract's code runs. If it calls back into your contract before you have finished updating your records, it can withdraw again and again. Study this vulnerable example, and then the fix.

The problem is the order: the contract sends the money before it sets the balance to zero. A malicious contract receiving the money can call withdraw() again from its receive function, while its balance still reads as non-zero.

Defences

  • Follow checks-effects-interactions.
  • Use a reentrancy guard (a lock) on functions that send value.
  • Prefer pulling payments (users withdraw) to pushing them to many addresses.
  • Keep external calls to a minimum and treat every external address as untrusted.
  • Have the code audited.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the key fix for the vulnerable bank?
  • Update the balance before sending the ETH (correct)
  • Charge more gas
  • Remove the owner
  • Use tx.origin

Effects before interactions.

Check what you just learned

1. In checks-effects-interactions, external calls come:
  • First
  • Last (correct)
  • Never
  • In the middle

After state is updated.
keyPoints: Reentrancy happens when an external call lets an attacker call back before state is updated.
Checks, effects, interactions prevents it.

topics.title: What contracts cannot do
topics.html:
Limits to design around
LimitWhat it meansWorkaround
No true randomnessBlock data can be influenced by producersUse a verifiable randomness service
No outside dataContracts cannot make web requestsUse an oracle
No schedulingContracts cannot wake themselves upUse an off-chain keeper or let users trigger actions
Limited storage and gasBig loops and big data are too expensiveDesign for small bounded operations; keep big data off-chain
ImmutabilityBugs cannot be patched easilyTest heavily; consider carefully governed upgrades; include a pause
Public dataEverything on-chain is visible, including 'private' variablesNever store secrets in a contract
Watch out

The private keyword only stops other contracts from reading a variable directly. Anyone can read all contract storage from a node. Never put passwords or secrets on-chain.

Common mistakes

  • Looping over an array that can grow without limit, so one day the transaction costs more than the block allows.
  • Using block.timestamp for fine-grained decisions or randomness.
  • Assuming 'private' means secret.
  • Skipping tests because the code is 'simple'.

Check what you just learned

1. Does the private keyword hide data from everyone?
  • Yes
  • Only on test networks
  • No, it only restricts other contracts' direct access (correct)
  • Only for owners

All storage is readable.

Check what you just learned

1. Smart contracts cannot by themselves:
  • Hold ETH
  • Store numbers
  • Emit events
  • Fetch web data (correct)

They need an oracle.

Key terms: flip and sort

Access control
Rules about who may call a function
revert
Undo the transaction with an error
Reentrancy
Calling back into a contract before it updates its state
Checks-effects-interactions
A safe ordering of operations
Reentrancy guard
A lock that blocks nested calls
Oracle
A source of outside data
keyPoints: No randomness, no outside data, no self-scheduling, limited gas and public storage.
private is not secret.

modules.title: Testing and deploying
modules.summary: Test networks, automated tests, verification and a deployment checklist.
modules.outcome: You can run a test, deploy to a test network, verify source code and follow a checklist before going live.
modules.intro: Because a deployed contract is hard to change, professional teams spend more time testing than coding. This last module introduces automated tests, test networks and the discipline of a deployment checklist.

topics.title: Automated tests
topics.html:
Instead of clicking through Remix every time, developers write tests: small programs that deploy the contract to a local blockchain, call it, and check the results. Popular tools include Hardhat and Foundry. The following example uses Hardhat with JavaScript to test the TipJar contract. You can run it on your own computer after installing Node.js and Hardhat; the course platform itself does not run code.

What the test shows
LineMeaning
ethers.getSigners()Gets test accounts with fake ETH
ethers.deployContract("TipJar")Deploys a fresh contract for the test
jar.connect(fan).tip({ value: ... })Calls tip() as the fan, sending 0.1 ETH
expect(...).to.equal(...)Asserts an exact result
revertedWithCustomError(jar, "NotOwner")Asserts that a non-owner is rejected with the expected error
to.emit(jar, "Withdrawn")Asserts that the event was logged

What to test

  • The happy path for every function.
  • Every revert and every access-control rule.
  • Edge cases: zero amounts, maximum values, repeated calls.
  • Events: that they are emitted with the right data.
  • Sequences: tip, tip, withdraw, tip again.

Check what you just learned

1. Why test the failing paths as well?
  • Because attackers will try them (correct)
  • To make tests longer
  • They are free
  • Because law requires it

Security lives in the rejected cases.

Check what you just learned

1. A good test suite checks:
  • Only successes
  • Successes and failures (correct)
  • Only events
  • Nothing

Failures matter most.
keyPoints: Automated tests deploy and call contracts on a local chain.
Test reverts and access control, not just the happy path.

topics.title: Test networks and verification
topics.html:
Why each step
StepPurpose
Local testsFast feedback and no cost
Test networkRealistic environment: real tools, real timing, fake money
Source verificationLets users and auditors read exactly what runs
Small first deploymentLimits the harm of a surprise
MonitoringAlerts you to unusual activity
Definition

Verification. Publishing a contract's source code and compiler settings to a block explorer, which recompiles it and confirms that the result matches the deployed bytecode. Verified contracts can be read and checked by anyone.

Tip

Keep the deployment addresses, the constructor arguments and the compiler version in a file in your project. You will need them again.

Check what you just learned

1. Why deploy to a test network before the main network?
  • It is required by law
  • It is faster
  • To find problems with fake money (correct)
  • It lowers gas on mainnet

Mistakes are free there.

Check what you just learned

1. Verifying a contract means:
  • Making it faster
  • Changing the owner
  • Hiding the code
  • Publishing source that matches the deployed bytecode (correct)

Transparency.
keyPoints: Test, then testnet, then verify, then small, then monitor.
Verification lets anyone read the deployed code.

topics.title: A pre-launch checklist
topics.html:
Before going live

  1. All tests pass, including failure cases.
  2. The code has been read by a second person.
  3. For anything holding real money, an independent audit is complete and findings are fixed.
  4. Owner keys are held in a hardware wallet or a multi-signature wallet.
  5. There is an emergency plan: who can pause, and how will you tell users?
  6. The source is verified and the addresses are documented.
  7. Start with limits on how much value the contract can hold.
Common launch mistakes
MistakeBetter
Deploying with a hot wallet that also does daily workA dedicated deployer key, then transfer ownership to a safer wallet
No pause or limitsAdd a pause and deposit caps for the first weeks
Skipping an audit to save moneyBudget for review; losses are larger than audit fees
No monitoringAlerts on large transfers and owner actions
Silence during an incidentA status page and clear updates
Watch out

This course teaches concepts and good habits, not a guarantee that code is secure. For any contract that will hold real value, hire experienced auditors and follow current security guidance.

Check what you just learned

1. Why add deposit limits in the first weeks?
  • To limit the harm if a bug is found (correct)
  • To make it look busy
  • To save gas
  • To avoid events

A cap limits the blast radius.

Check what you just learned

1. The first deployment to a real network should hold:
  • As much as possible
  • A small, capped amount (correct)
  • Nothing ever
  • Borrowed funds

Start small.

Key terms: flip and sort

Hardhat
A development environment for Ethereum
Foundry
Another toolkit written for speed
Unit test
A small automated check of one behaviour
Testnet
A network with worthless coins for practice
Verification
Publishing source that matches the bytecode
Audit
An independent security review
keyPoints: Test, review, audit, secure keys, plan for incidents and limit exposure.
Audits and professional help are needed for real value.
